sections.title: The hook
sections.intro_md:
Every year around April, when the Salaulim reservoir in South Goa drops low enough, a village climbs out of the water. Curdi was flooded when the dam filled. For a few weeks its old roads, house plinths, a temple and a chapel stand in the sun, and families who were moved out more than 40 years ago come back to walk them. Then the monsoon arrives and Curdi goes under again.

Goa does this a lot: the past keeps resurfacing. A Jesuit saint who died in 1552 still lies in a silver casket in Old Goa, and about 8 million people queued to see him in 2024 and 2025. Portugal ruled the coast for 451 years and left vindaloo, bread, carnival and a civil code. India took it back in 36 hours in December 1961. Goans then voted, in India's only referendum of its kind, not to be swallowed by Maharashtra.

Today: the smallest state, the second richest per head, and 10.8 million tourists a year in a place of 1.5 million people.

sections.title: Where you are
sections.intro_md:
Goa sits on India's west coast, between Maharashtra to the north and Karnataka to the east and south. It is the smallest state by area, 3,702 square kilometres, less than a tenth of Kerala. You can drive from the northern border at the Terekhol river to the southern one at Polem in about three hours.

The 2011 Census counted 1,458,545 people. It became India's 25th state on 30 May 1987, after 26 years as a Union Territory with Daman and Diu. The capital is Panaji (Panjim). The biggest towns are Vasco da Gama, Margao, Mapusa and Ponda. Since 31 December 2025 there are three districts: North Goa, South Goa and the new Kushavati, carved from the south.

The one language in the law is Konkani in Devanagari script. Money comes from tourists, iron ore (when the mines are open), pharmaceuticals and remittances. Per person, Goans earn nearly three times the Indian average.

sections.title: The land
sections.intro_md:
Goa is a staircase from the Western Ghats down to the Arabian Sea. The eastern third is forested hills, up to about 1,000 metres, where the rain falls hardest and the iron ore lies. The middle is laterite plateau, the red rock Goans cut into bricks for houses, forts and churches. The western edge is river mouths, mangroves, paddy and beach.

Seven rivers cross this short distance. The Mandovi and the Zuari are the big two, joined by the Cumbarjua canal so that the islands of Tiswadi are surrounded by water. Saltwater pushes far inland on the tide. Over centuries farmers built khazans, walled fields with sluice gates that let fish in and keep salt out.

About 56 percent of the state is forest or tree cover. Monsoon rain, about 3,000 millimetres a year, turns the whole state green from June to September and empties the beaches.

spotlights.name: Dudhsagar Falls
spotlights.spot_it: A white, four-tiered fall on a jungle cliff, with a railway bridge running straight across its face.
spotlights.story_md: Dudhsagar means 'sea of milk'. The Mandovi drops about 310 metres here in four tiers, which puts it among India's tallest falls. The strangest thing is the railway: the line from Londa to Vasco crosses the face of the falls on a stone bridge, so trains pass through the spray. It was built by the West of India Portuguese Railway in the 1880s to carry goods to Mormugao. In the monsoon the falls are at their best and the forest roads are closed, so the classic view is from a train window. In the dry months jeeps take visitors up from Collem.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's best-known landscape outside the beaches, and the reason a railway runs through a waterfall.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sea of milk with a train running through the froth.

spotlights.name: The Mandovi river
spotlights.when: Rises in the Ghats of Karnataka
spotlights.spot_it: A broad brown estuary with casino boats moored off Panaji and ferries crossing to Betim.
spotlights.story_md: The Mandovi, also called Mhadei, runs about 77 kilometres, most of it in Goa. It made Goa: Old Goa, the Portuguese capital, sat on its bank, and Panaji replaced it at the mouth. Iron ore barges once crowded it day and night. Now floating casinos are moored offshore, because gambling licences in Goa were tied to offshore vessels. Upstream, Goa and Karnataka have argued for decades over Karnataka's plan to divert Mhadei water to the Malaprabha basin. A 2018 tribunal award gave Karnataka 13.4 thousand million cubic feet and Goa 24; all sides appealed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's main river and its longest-running dispute with a neighbour.
spotlights.memory_hook: Old Goa lived on it, Panaji drinks from it, Karnataka wants a share.

spotlights.name: Khazan lands

where.label: Estuaries of Tiswadi, Salcete and Bardez

spotlights.spot_it: Flat paddy fields below river level, ringed by mud bunds, with wooden sluice gates at the water's edge.
spotlights.story_md: Khazans are fields reclaimed from estuary mud. Villagers built earthen bunds against the tide and fitted sluice gates (manos) that open and close with the water. In the monsoon the fields grow salt-tolerant rice; in the dry season the gates let in fish and prawns, which are trapped and auctioned. The bunds were maintained collectively by the village communidade, an association of founding families older than Portuguese rule. Many khazans have broken down since the 1970s as farm labour left and land was sold, and the salt has come back in.
spotlights.why_it_matters: An engineering system shared by a whole village, now mostly abandoned.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fields below the river, kept dry by a door that opens with the tide.

spotlights.name: Chorao mangroves and the Salim Ali sanctuary
spotlights.spot_it: Dense green mangroves on a tidal island, a boardwalk, mudskippers hopping on the mud at low tide.
spotlights.story_md: Chorao is an island in the Mandovi a ferry ride from Panaji. Its western tip is the Salim Ali Bird Sanctuary, named after India's best-known ornithologist and only about 1.8 square kilometres. Mangroves here trap silt, shelter fish nurseries and blunt storm surges. At low tide the mud fills with fiddler crabs waving one oversized claw, and mudskippers, fish that breathe through their skin and walk on their fins. Herons, kingfishers and crocodiles share the creeks. Canoe trips go in at high tide.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most accessible mangrove forest in Goa, minutes from the capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fish that walks, a crab that waves, a sanctuary you reach by ferry.

spotlights.name: Palolem
spotlights.spot_it: A perfect crescent of sand with palms right to the edge, rocky headlands at both ends, huts on stilts.
spotlights.story_md: Palolem is a curved bay about a kilometre long in Canacona, the far south. Calm water makes it one of the few Goan beaches good for swimming most of the season. The huts are temporary: by law, beach shacks and huts come down before the monsoon and go back up in October. At the north end, Canacona Island is reachable on foot at low tide. Palolem is where many visitors find the Goa of postcards, though in December it is as busy as anywhere.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The south's best-known beach and the model of the seasonal shack economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: A moon-shaped beach that is rebuilt every October.

spotlights.name: Curdi, the village under the reservoir
spotlights.when: Re-emerges about April to May each year
spotlights.spot_it: Cracked mud flats with stone plinths, a temple and chapel ruins, and people walking where water stood weeks before.
spotlights.story_md: Curdi was a farming village of Hindus and Catholics in Sanguem. In the 1970s and 1980s the Salaulim dam, pushed by Goa's first Chief Minister Dayanand Bandodkar to supply water to South Goa, flooded it. About 3,000 people were resettled, mostly in Valkinim and Vaddem. Each summer the reservoir drops and the old village appears. Former residents return for the Someshwar temple festival and a chapel Mass. Visitors look for the ruined house of the singer Mogubai Kurdikar, who was born here and whose daughter was Kishori Amonkar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A reminder that Goa's water supply cost a whole village.
spotlights.memory_hook: A village with a once-a-year address.

sections.title: People by numbers
sections.intro_md:
Goa is small and dense, about 394 people per square kilometre in 2011, and it is the most urban big state in India: more than 62 percent of Goans lived in towns in 2011. Literacy was 88.7 percent. The sex ratio was 973 women per 1,000 men.

Religion is the number most visitors get wrong. Goa is not a Christian state. In 2011, 66.1 percent were Hindu, 25.1 percent Christian and 8.3 percent Muslim. The Christian share was much higher under Portugal and fell after 1961 as people from other states moved in and many Catholic Goans emigrated.

Emigration is a Goan habit. Goans have worked as cooks, clerks and musicians in Bombay, as civil servants in Portuguese Africa, as seafarers on cruise lines and in the Gulf. Goans born before 19 December 1961, and their descendants, can register as Portuguese citizens, and tens of thousands have done so to work in Britain and the rest of Europe.

sections.title: Before the Portuguese
sections.intro_md:
Goa's written history starts long before 1510. The Mauryas, the Satavahanas and the Bhojas held this coast. In the Puranas, the hero Parashurama shoots an arrow into the sea and the water draws back to give him the Konkan, a story Goans still tell about their land.

From about 960 to the mid-1300s the Kadambas of Goa ruled from Chandor and then from Gopakapattana, a port on the Zuari near modern Goa Velha. They traded with Arabia and East Africa, minted gold coins and built temples in stone. Delhi Sultanate raids in the 1300s broke them. Vijayanagara and the Bahmani sultans fought over the port for horses, the key import of the age: whoever held Goa controlled the trade in Arabian war horses for the Deccan.

By 1500 Goa belonged to Yusuf Adil Shah, sultan of Bijapur, who built a palace in the city now called Old Goa.

spotlights.name: Usgalimal rock engravings
spotlights.spot_it: Shallow outlines of bulls, deer, a peacock and human figures scratched into flat laterite on a riverbank.
spotlights.story_md: In 1993 villagers led archaeologists to a bend in the Kushavati where monsoon floods had washed mud off a sheet of laterite. Underneath were more than 100 engravings: humped bulls, antelope, a peacock, dancing figures and a labyrinth pattern. Nobody agrees how old they are. Estimates run from about 4,000 years to 20,000 or 30,000 years, because there is nothing datable in the rock itself and scholars compare styles with other sites. What is not in dispute: they are the oldest art in Goa, and the river that guarded them now names Goa's newest district.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that people were drawing in Goa thousands of years before any temple or church.
spotlights.memory_hook: A flood uncovered them; a district took the river's name.

spotlights.name: Mahadev temple, Tambdi Surla
spotlights.spot_it: A small, dark grey basalt temple in deep forest, with a stepped tower and a pillared porch.
spotlights.story_md: This is the only Kadamba-era temple in Goa that survives more or less intact. Its builders used basalt, which had to be carried in from elsewhere, because Goa's local laterite crumbles too easily for fine carving. The forest location saved it. When Portuguese viceroys ordered temples in the coastal Old Conquests destroyed in the 1540s and later, they never reached this deep into the hills, and Muslim raiders before them missed it too. Inside the hall, a carved king cobra on a ceiling panel and lotus patterns are still crisp after about 800 years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's oldest standing temple, and a clue to how much was lost elsewhere.
spotlights.memory_hook: The temple that survived because nobody could find it.

spotlights.name: Kadamba gold pagoda coin
spotlights.spot_it: A small, thick gold coin with a lion on one side and Devanagari letters, only about 16 millimetres across.
spotlights.story_md: The Kadambas of Goa grew rich on sea trade. Arab merchants lived in their port of Gopakapattana, and one, a Muslim named Sadhan, was a minister. The kings minted gold 'pagodas', small heavy coins weighing about 3 grams, often stamped with a lion, their emblem, and a royal title in Devanagari. This one names a king as 'conqueror of the Malavas'. Kadamba coins are among the earliest hard evidence of Goa as a wealthy, outward-looking port, centuries before Vasco da Gama.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's trade wealth is older than Portugal: here it is in gold.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lion in gold, 3 grams of proof that Goa was rich before Portugal.

spotlights.name: Safa Masjid
spotlights.spot_it: A modest mosque with a sloping tiled roof beside a large stone-lined tank with arched niches.
spotlights.story_md: Ibrahim Adil Shah of Bijapur built the Safa Shahouri Masjid at Ponda in 1560, when Ponda was still outside Portuguese territory. It is the best-preserved early mosque in Goa. The large tank beside it, lined with laterite and pointed arches, was for ablutions. Gardens and fountains once surrounded it. Most other mosques of the period in the Portuguese zone were destroyed, which makes this small building, protected today by the Archaeological Survey of India, a rare survivor of Goa's Muslim centuries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The main surviving trace of the Adil Shahi sultans who ruled Goa before Portugal.
spotlights.memory_hook: The sultan's mosque that stood just outside Portugal's reach.

sections.title: Four and a half centuries of Portugal
sections.intro_md:
Afonso de Albuquerque took Goa from Bijapur in March 1510, lost it, and took it back for good on 25 November 1510, the feast of St Catherine. Portugal wanted a base to control the Indian Ocean spice and horse trade, and Goa's island city became the capital of an empire stretching from Mozambique to Macau.

By the late 1500s Old Goa was one of the largest cities in Asia, called the Rome of the East, packed with churches, convents and a hospital. The price was high. From the 1540s temples in the Old Conquests were destroyed and Hindu rites banned. The Inquisition ran from 1560 to 1812. Many Hindu families moved their gods across the river into Ponda, outside Portuguese control.

Then Old Goa died. Cholera, malaria and the silting of the Mandovi emptied it in the 1600s and 1700s. The capital moved to Panaji, formally in 1843. In 1763 to 1788 Portugal added the inland New Conquests, but by then it was more tolerant, so those areas stayed mostly Hindu.

spotlights.name: Afonso de Albuquerque
spotlights.spot_it: In portraits: a long white beard to the chest, black clothes, a hard stare.
spotlights.story_md: Albuquerque was the strategist of Portugal's Asian empire. He seized Goa, Malacca and Hormuz to control the sea lanes. In Goa he married his soldiers to local women, mostly widows of the defeated Muslim garrison, to create a settled population loyal to Portugal, and he abolished sati in Portuguese territory. He also massacred the Muslim defenders after the second capture. Legend says he swore never to shave until he had taken the Red Sea. He died at sea off Goa in December 1515, after learning he had been replaced as governor.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The man who turned a port into the capital of a sea empire.
spotlights.memory_hook: A beard he would not cut and a city he would not give back.

spotlights.name: Basilica of Bom Jesus
spotlights.spot_it: A dark red, unplastered laterite facade with columns in three styles stacked one above another.
spotlights.story_md: Bom Jesus means 'Good Jesus' or 'Infant Jesus'. The Jesuits built it between 1594 and 1605. Every other major church in Old Goa is whitewashed; Bom Jesus lost its lime plaster in the 1950s when conservators stripped it, and the raw laterite became its signature. Its facade mixes Doric, Ionic and Corinthian columns, a lesson in classical orders. It holds the body of St Francis Xavier. In 1986 UNESCO listed it with the other churches and convents of Goa as a World Heritage Site, and in 1946 it became the first church in India raised to minor basilica.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most visited building in Goa and the heart of Catholic Goa.
spotlights.memory_hook: The red church: plaster off, saint inside.

spotlights.name: The body of St Francis Xavier

where.label: Basilica of Bom Jesus, Old Goa

spotlights.spot_it: A silver casket with glass sides on a carved marble tomb in a side chapel.
spotlights.story_md: Francis Xavier, a Spanish Jesuit, arrived in Goa in 1542 and died on Shangchuan island off China in 1552. His body, buried in quicklime, was found intact months later and reached Goa in 1554. Bits of it have travelled: his right forearm went to Rome in 1614. The silver casket was made by Goan silversmiths in 1636 and 1637; the marble tomb was a gift from Cosimo III de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, installed in 1698. About every ten years the body is shown publicly. The 18th exposition, from 21 November 2024 to 5 January 2025, drew an estimated 8 million people.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's patron saint, and its biggest single crowd event.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Spanish saint, a Goan casket, a Florentine tomb, and 8 million visitors.

spotlights.name: Se Cathedral
spotlights.spot_it: A huge, whitewashed Portuguese-Manueline church with one square bell tower; the other side is missing.
spotlights.story_md: The Se is dedicated to St Catherine of Alexandria, because Albuquerque took Goa on her feast day. It took 57 years to build and is about 76 metres long, one of the largest churches in Asia. Its tower holds the Golden Bell, said to be the largest in Goa; its sound was famous enough to be used to signal Inquisition sentences. The cathedral once had two towers. One collapsed in 1776 and was never rebuilt, which gives the facade its lopsided look. It is still the seat of the Archbishop of Goa and Daman.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The mother church of Portuguese Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: One tower, one bell, one very big church.

spotlights.name: Asia's first printing press and Garcia de Orta
spotlights.spot_it: A plain Portuguese title page: Coloquios dos simples, e drogas he cousas mediçinais da India, Goa, 1563.
spotlights.story_md: In 1556 a ship carrying a printing press to Ethiopia stopped in Goa and never left. Jesuits set it up at St Paul's College, making it the first press in India and among the first in Asia. Its most famous book came in 1563: Garcia de Orta's Colloquies on the Simples and Drugs of India. Orta, a Portuguese Jewish physician, described more than 50 plants and drugs, including the first European account of cholera in India. Because he was of Jewish descent, the Inquisition later dug up his bones and burned them, in 1580.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa printed books in India 250 years before most of the country.
spotlights.memory_hook: Printed in Goa in 1563; the author's bones burned in 1580.

spotlights.name: The Goa Inquisition
spotlights.spot_it: No monument survives: the palace of the Inquisition in Old Goa was demolished, and its records burned.
spotlights.story_md: The Inquisition was set up in Goa in 1560 at the request of Francis Xavier, among others. It targeted New Christians accused of secretly practising Judaism, converts who kept Hindu or Muslim customs, and anyone who used Hindu rituals at weddings or funerals. Wearing a dhoti or cooking rice without salt, a Hindu habit, could be evidence. Estimates of trials run to about 16,000, with hundreds executed, but the archive was mostly destroyed after 1812, so exact numbers are disputed. It was suspended in 1774, revived in 1778 and abolished in 1812.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shaped who left Goa, who converted, and why Ponda is full of temples.
spotlights.memory_hook: A court that could convict you for cooking rice without salt.

spotlights.name: Fort Aguada
spotlights.spot_it: Massive laterite walls on a headland at the mouth of the Mandovi, a white lighthouse tower inside.
spotlights.story_md: Aguada means 'watering place'. The Portuguese built the fort in 1612 against the Dutch, who were then attacking Portuguese bases across Asia. Ships coming in called here for fresh water from a spring inside the walls; the cistern held about 2.4 million gallons. The 1864 lighthouse was one of the oldest of its kind in Asia. The lower fort later became a jail, closed in 2015 and turned into a museum of the freedom struggle. Two Indian naval officers died in the fighting here on 19 December 1961.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Dutch never took it, and it watered every ship to Goa.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fort built to fight the Dutch and remembered for the water.

sections.title: Liberation and the vote
sections.intro_md:
When India became independent in 1947, Portugal refused to leave. Its dictator, Antonio Salazar, declared Goa an overseas province, legally part of Portugal. Goans had resisted for centuries, from the Pinto conspiracy of 1787 to Tristao de Braganza Cunha's nationalist writing in the 1920s and 1930s. On 18 June 1946 the socialist Ram Manohar Lohia broke a ban on public meetings in Margao; that day is still Goa Revolution Day.

In the 1950s satyagrahis marched across the border and some were shot. Nehru waited 14 years, then sent the army. Operation Vijay began on 18 December 1961. In about 36 hours the Portuguese governor, Manuel Antonio Vassalo e Silva, surrendered, against Salazar's orders to fight to the last man. 19 December is Liberation Day.

One question was left: should Goa join Maharashtra? On 16 January 1967 Goans voted. The answer was no.

spotlights.name: Operation Vijay
spotlights.spot_it: Archive film of Indian troops riding into Panaji to cheering crowds; a Portuguese sloop beached and burning at Mormugao.
spotlights.story_md: India sent about 30,000 troops against about 3,500 Portuguese. The Air Force bombed the Dabolim airfield and the Bambolim wireless station; the Navy attacked the sloop NRP Afonso de Albuquerque, which was run aground; the Army crossed from the north and east. Salazar ordered his commander to resist and expected martyrs. Governor Vassalo e Silva signed the surrender instead on the evening of 19 December, saving Goa from destruction. Portugal court-martialled him. Portugal recognised Indian sovereignty only in 1974, after its own revolution.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ended 451 years of European rule in about a day and a half.
spotlights.memory_hook: 36 hours to end 451 years.

spotlights.name: The Opinion Poll
spotlights.spot_it: No picture needed: Goans remember it as Asmitai Dis, Identity Day, every 16 January.
spotlights.story_md: The first elected government of Goa, under Dayanand Bandodkar's Maharashtrawadi Gomantak Party, wanted to merge Goa into Maharashtra, arguing that Konkani was a dialect of Marathi. Jack de Sequeira's United Goans Party pushed for a direct vote instead. Parliament passed a special law and on 16 January 1967 Goans voted, with turnout of about 82 percent. 172,191 voted to stay separate, 138,170 to merge. It is the only time an Indian state's fate was put to a direct popular vote. Without it there would be no Goa state, no Konkani state language, and possibly no Goan identity as we know it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goans chose to stay Goan.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 34,021-vote margin that saved a state.

sections.title: Konkani, in five scripts
sections.intro_md:
Konkani is an Indo-Aryan language spoken along the Konkan coast from southern Maharashtra to Kerala. Goa is its home. For a long time it was looked down on: the Portuguese pushed Portuguese, and Marathi was the language of Hindu schooling and temple scripture, so Konkani was treated as a kitchen tongue.

That changed in stages. The Sahitya Akademi recognised Konkani as an independent literary language in 1975. The Goa, Daman and Diu Official Language Act of 1987 made Konkani in Devanagari the official language, with Marathi allowed for official purposes. In 1992 Konkani was added to the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.

Konkani is unusual: it is written in five scripts. Devanagari in Goa's official use, Roman script (Romi) by Goan Catholics and in tiatr, Kannada script in Karnataka, Malayalam script in Kerala, and Perso-Arabic by the Nawayath Muslims of Bhatkal. The script you use often tells your religion and region.

spotlights.name: Doutrina Christam and Thomas Stephens
spotlights.spot_it: A small printed catechism with a Portuguese title page, the Konkani inside written in Roman letters.
spotlights.story_md: Thomas Stephens was an English Jesuit who arrived in Goa in 1579, probably the first Englishman to live in India. He learned Konkani and Marathi and wrote the Kristapurana, a life of Christ in about 11,000 verses in Marathi in the style of Hindu puranas. His Doutrina Christam em Lingoa Bramana Canarim, printed in 1622, is the first printed book in Konkani. He also wrote the first Konkani grammar. A Jesuit, writing for converts, made Konkani a printed language.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first printed book in Konkani was made by an Englishman.
spotlights.memory_hook: Konkani's first book had an English author and a Portuguese title.

sections.title: Temples, churches and a mosque
sections.intro_md:
Goan Hindu temples look like nobody else's. Many deities fled the Old Conquests in the 1500s and were re-installed across the rivers in Ponda, Bicholim and Pernem, then under friendlier rulers. When the temples were rebuilt in the 1700s, often with Maratha money, builders borrowed from churches: domes, arched windows, chandeliers, and a tall lamp tower, the deepastambha, that plays the role of a bell tower.

Many Goan Catholics still know which Hindu family deity, or kuldevta, their ancestors worshipped, and the old caste names, Bamon and Chardo, survive among Catholics too. Hindu and Catholic villages share festivals, foods and sometimes saints.

The Catholic year runs on feasts: every village church has one, with a Mass, a fair and a band. The biggest is St Francis Xavier on 3 December.

pins.label: Bom Jesus and Se, Old Goa

spotlights.name: Shri Mangueshi temple
spotlights.spot_it: A white temple with an octagonal dome, a seven-storey lamp tower in the courtyard and a tank in front.
spotlights.story_md: Mangesh, a form of Shiva, was worshipped at Kutthal in Salcete. When the Portuguese began destroying temples there around 1560, the Saraswat devotees carried the linga across the Zuari to Priol, in territory ruled from Bijapur and later the Sonda kings. The present temple dates from the 1700s, built with Maratha patronage. The family of the musician Dinanath Mangeshkar came from Mangeshi village and took its name, so Lata Mangeshkar's surname points to this temple.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best-known of Ponda's refugee temples.
spotlights.memory_hook: A god who crossed a river to stay safe, and gave a singer her surname.

spotlights.name: Shri Shantadurga temple
spotlights.spot_it: A pink and white temple with a pyramidal tiered roof, a dome and a tall white lamp tower ringed with oil-lamp ledges.
spotlights.story_md: Shantadurga is Durga as the peacemaker: the story says she stood between Shiva and Vishnu during a quarrel and calmed them. Her original shrine at Quelossim was destroyed in 1564 and the deity was moved to Kavlem. The present temple was built in 1738 with money from Naroram Mantri, a minister of the Maratha ruler Shahu. Its deepastambha is lit with hundreds of oil lamps at festivals. Look at the interior: chandeliers and arched windows that a Portuguese church builder would recognise.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The clearest example of Goa's temple style, half Maratha, half Baroque.
spotlights.memory_hook: The goddess who made peace, in a temple that borrowed from churches.

spotlights.name: Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, Panaji
spotlights.spot_it: A brilliant white Baroque church at the top of a zigzag staircase in the centre of Panaji.
spotlights.story_md: This was the first church sailors saw when they came up the Mandovi from Lisbon, and they stopped here to give thanks before going on to Old Goa. The zigzag stairs were added in the 1870s. In the tower hangs a large bell that once belonged to the Augustinian church in Old Goa, brought here after that church was abandoned. The church is the backdrop of Panaji: the feast on 8 December fills the square with a fair.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The postcard church of Goa's capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lisbon's sailors said thank you here before docking.

spotlights.name: Lairai jatra and the firewalk
spotlights.when: Annually in late April or May
spotlights.spot_it: Devotees called dhonds, dressed in white and holding canes, walk barefoot across a bed of glowing embers before dawn.
spotlights.story_md: The goddess Lairai is said to be one of seven sisters in Goan legend. At her annual jatra in Shirgao, thousands of devotees who have fasted for days walk across hot coals. In the early hours of 3 May 2025 a crowd of tens of thousands surged on a slope near the temple and six people died in a crush; reports of injured ranged from 30 to about 80. An inquiry blamed crowd management. The firewalk continues, with new controls.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A living ritual that also shows the risks of Goa's crowded festivals.
spotlights.memory_hook: Barefoot on coals, at a festival that turned deadly in 2025.

sections.title: Houses with a balcao
sections.intro_md:
The Goan house is the most recognisable thing on the landscape after the churches. Wealthy Catholic and Hindu families in the 1800s built houses facing the street, not hidden behind walls: a raised plinth, a covered porch with built-in seats called the balcao, tall windows, carved pillars, and colours that are often bright yellow, blue, green or red, with white trim.

Under Portuguese rule, it is often said, owners had to paint their houses every year after the monsoon or pay a fine. Whether the law existed in that form is not clear, but the habit of bright paint is real. Many grand houses were built with money earned abroad, in Bombay, Africa and Lisbon.

Since 2000 many have been sold, split among heirs who live overseas, or left to rot. Others have become boutique hotels.

rows.Chandor country mansion: Dozens of rooms, a long facade

spotlights.name: Fontainhas
spotlights.spot_it: Narrow lanes of yellow, blue and ochre houses with red tile roofs, wrought-iron balconies and blue-and-white tile name plates.
spotlights.story_md: Fontainhas, the 'little fountains', is Panaji's old Latin quarter at the foot of Altinho hill. It grew in the late 1700s on land reclaimed by a Goan who had made his money in Mozambique, António João de Sequeira. The name comes from the Phoenix spring at its edge. Look for azulejos, painted ceramic tiles, used for house names and street signs, and for small chapels, including the Chapel of St Sebastian with a crucifix that once hung in the Inquisition's palace. Expect cameras: it is the most photographed street in Goa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best-preserved Portuguese-era neighbourhood in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Little fountains, loud colours, every house with a tiled name.

spotlights.name: Menezes Braganza house
spotlights.spot_it: A long two-storey mansion on Chandor's church square, 28 windows across the front.
spotlights.story_md: Chandor was once the Kadamba capital. The Braganza house there is two houses in one: the family split it into an east wing and a west wing. One side has a ballroom with Belgian chandeliers and Italian marble, and a library of about 5,000 books gathered by the journalist Luis de Menezes Braganza, who opposed Portuguese rule. The family chapel holds a fingernail said to be from St Francis Xavier. Members of the family still live here and show visitors round for a donation.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The grandest private house in Goa, still lived in.
spotlights.memory_hook: One house, two wings, one saint's fingernail.

spotlights.name: Oyster-shell windows

where.label: Old houses and churches across Goa

spotlights.spot_it: Small square panes in a wooden window frame, pearly and translucent, letting in soft light but no view.
spotlights.story_md: Glass was expensive in Portuguese Goa, so builders used the flat, thin shell of the windowpane oyster, Placuna placenta, which grows in the shallows of Goan estuaries. Polished and cut into squares about 5 centimetres across, the shells are translucent: they let in a soft, pearly light and keep out the glare and much of the heat. Many old houses and churches still have them. The oyster is now protected under India's wildlife law, and replacement shells are scarce.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's local answer to glass, and a reason old rooms feel cool and dim.
spotlights.memory_hook: Windows made from oysters.

sections.title: Mando, ghumot and tiatr
sections.intro_md:
Goa has given India more musicians per head than almost anywhere. Goan Catholic boys learned violin and solfege in parish schools from the 1600s; by the 20th century Goans played in every dance band in Bombay and arranged music for Hindi films. Hindu Goa supplied classical singers: Kesarbai Kerkar, Mogubai Kurdikar, Kishori Amonkar, and the Mangeshkar family.

At home, folk forms divide roughly by community. Catholic Goa has the mando, a slow love song in Konkani; the faster dulpod; and the dekhni, which mixes Indian and Western music. Hindu Goa has the fugdi, the women's circle dance, and the drum-led processions of Shigmo. One instrument crosses both: the ghumot, a clay pot drum.

The popular stage is tiatr, Konkani musical theatre. It runs year-round in village halls, often for three hours.

rows.Mando: Women in the pano bhaju, men in suits

spotlights.name: Mando
spotlights.spot_it: A slow Konkani song in waltz time with violin and ghumot; couples move gracefully, the women waving fans or handkerchiefs.
spotlights.story_md: The mando grew in Goan Catholic homes in the 19th century. Its words are Konkani, often about love, separation or political events; its melody and harmony lean on European music; its beat comes from the ghumot. A mando is usually followed by a faster dulpod. In performance, women wear the pano bhaju, a Konkani adaptation of the Portuguese dress, and men wear suits. The All Goa Mando Festival, held since 1966 at Panaji, keeps it alive as a competition with categories for new songs and dance.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's signature song form, made from two continents.
spotlights.memory_hook: European waltz, Konkani words, a clay drum underneath.

spotlights.name: Ghumot
spotlights.spot_it: A clay pot with both ends open and skin stretched over the wider mouth, held under one arm and slapped with both palms.
spotlights.story_md: The ghumot is a clay drum. One end is covered with skin; the player strikes it with one hand and opens or closes the narrow end with the other to change the pitch. Hindu Goans play it at Shigmo and at Ganesh aarti; Catholic Goans play it under the mando. The skin was traditionally that of the monitor lizard, which is protected under wildlife law, so makers switched to goat skin. In August 2019 the Goa government declared it the state's heritage instrument.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The one sound shared by Hindu and Catholic Goa.
spotlights.memory_hook: A water pot that became a drum that became a state symbol.

spotlights.name: Tiatr

where.label: First staged in Bombay, now all over Goa

spotlights.spot_it: A Konkani play where, between scenes, singers step in front of the curtain to sing songs that have nothing to do with the plot.
spotlights.story_md: Tiatr was born in Bombay, where many Goans worked. On Easter Sunday, 17 April 1892, Lucasinho Ribeiro staged Italian Bhurgo, adapted from an Italian opera, at the New Alfred Theatre. A tiatr has six or seven acts with two or three songs between each. These songs, kantaram, are often political satire, and tiatrists have been jailed and sued for them. Performances last about three hours, mostly in Romi Konkani. 17 April is Tiatr Day, and India Post issued stamps for it in 2018.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's people's theatre and its sharpest political commentary.
spotlights.memory_hook: Born in Bombay on Easter Sunday, sung between the scenes.

spotlights.name: Fugdi
spotlights.when: Performed at Ganesh Chaturthi and Dhalo
spotlights.spot_it: Women in nine-yard saris in a circle, singing, clapping and then spinning in pairs, faster and faster.
spotlights.story_md: Fugdi is danced by women, without instruments in its oldest form: the women sing and clap, and the rhythm comes from breath and feet. It is performed in the month of Bhadrapad around Ganesh Chaturthi and at Dhalo, a winter festival when women gather at night in the village square. The climax is the whirl: two women hold hands, cross arms and spin on the spot, sometimes until one drops out. The same dance, fugdi or phugdi, is known in the Konkan coast of Maharashtra.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The women's own dance, kept by women for women.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sing, clap, then spin until someone stops.

sections.title: Fish curry rice, and what Portugal added
sections.intro_md:
The Goan everyday meal is three words: xit kodi nustem, rice, curry and fish. Parboiled red rice, a coconut curry soured with kokum or tamarind, and fried mackerel or kingfish. Goans say a Goan who goes a day without fish feels ill.

Portugal changed the larder more than the recipes. From the Americas, via Portugal, came chilli, tomato, potato, cashew, papaya, pineapple and guava; India had none of them before the 1500s. From Portugal came vinegar, pork and bread made with yeast. Goan Catholic cooks combined them with Konkani technique. Goan Hindu Saraswat cooking, often vegetarian on certain days but very fond of fish, kept older flavours: coconut, kokum, teppal (Sichuan pepper's cousin) and jaggery.

The result is two kitchens sharing one coast: a Catholic one of vindaloo, sorpotel, cafreal and chourico, and a Hindu one of hooman (fish curry), tonak and khatkhatem.

spotlights.name: Fish curry rice
spotlights.spot_it: A thin, bright orange coconut curry over red rice, with a fried fish slice on the side.
spotlights.story_md: The curry is coconut ground with dried red chillies, coriander, turmeric and garlic, soured with kokum or tamarind, and cooked with mackerel, kingfish or prawns. The rice is ukde, parboiled red rice, which is plump and slightly nutty. It is the meal of fishermen, office workers and ministers alike, and the reason Goans watch fish prices like others watch petrol. The monsoon fishing ban from June to July sends prices soaring and freezers filling up.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The one dish every Goan, of every community, eats.
spotlights.memory_hook: Xit kodi nustem: rice, curry, fish, every day.

spotlights.name: Vindaloo
spotlights.spot_it: A dark red, tangy pork curry with a sharp vinegar smell; in Goa it is sour and garlicky before it is hot.
spotlights.story_md: Vindaloo comes from the Portuguese carne de vinha d'alhos, meat marinated in wine (vinho) and garlic (alhos). Goan cooks swapped wine for palm vinegar and added red Kashmiri chillies, which give colour more than fire. The name was heard by the British as 'vindaloo', and in curry houses in Britain it became the hottest dish on the menu, often with potatoes added because 'aloo' sounded like it was in the name. A Goan vindaloo has no potato.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the clearest food links between India and Europe.
spotlights.memory_hook: Vinha d'alhos: wine and garlic, not potatoes and fire.

spotlights.name: Xacuti
spotlights.spot_it: A thick brown curry with flecks of roasted coconut, usually chicken or lamb, smelling of poppy seeds and spice.
spotlights.story_md: Xacuti (sha-ku-tee) is the complicated one. Grated coconut is roasted dry until brown, then ground with as many as 15 or more roasted spices, including poppy seeds, star anise, cloves, cinnamon and dried red chillies. The result is darker and deeper than any everyday curry. Catholic and Hindu Goans both make it, with chicken or mutton, and some Hindu homes make a vegetarian version with mushrooms. It is the dish for feasts and Sunday lunch.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's most spice-heavy curry, shared by both communities.
spotlights.memory_hook: Roast the coconut till brown, then roast everything else.

spotlights.name: Sorpotel
spotlights.spot_it: A dark, vinegary stew of small cubes of pork and liver, eaten with sannas, the fluffy steamed rice cakes.
spotlights.story_md: Sorpotel comes from the Portuguese sarapatel, a dish that also travelled to Brazil. In Goa it is pork, liver and sometimes heart cut into small cubes, cooked in a vinegar and chilli masala and, traditionally, thickened with pig's blood. Like vindaloo, it gets better each day: families make a large pot before Christmas and reheat it for a week. It is eaten with sannas, rice cakes leavened with toddy, the coconut palm sap.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Christmas dish of Catholic Goa.
spotlights.memory_hook: Better on day three than day one.

spotlights.name: Cafreal
spotlights.spot_it: Chicken pieces coated in a bright green masala of coriander, chilli and ginger, pan-fried until charred at the edges.
spotlights.story_md: Cafreal is green, which no other Goan curry is. The name and dish are thought to come from Portuguese Africa, especially Mozambique, through soldiers and settlers who moved between the colonies. The word comes from cafre, an old Portuguese term for Africans now considered a slur. The marinade is fresh coriander, green chillies, ginger, garlic, lime and vinegar. It is served in bars with chips and bread, a classic of Goa's tavernas.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A dish that tells you Goa was part of an Africa-to-Asia empire.
spotlights.memory_hook: The green chicken that came from Mozambique.

spotlights.name: Chourico and pao
spotlights.when: Made in summer, eaten all year
spotlights.spot_it: Strings of small, round, dark red sausages tied like beads, sold hanging at the Friday market in Mapusa.
spotlights.story_md: Goan chourico is pork cured with salt, vinegar, chilli and spices, packed into casings, tied into strings and dried in the sun or smoked. It keeps for months, which mattered before refrigerators. It is fried with onions and eaten stuffed in pao, the soft Goan bread roll. Pao itself is a Portuguese legacy: the poder, the village baker, still rides a bicycle through Goan villages at dawn and in the afternoon with a basket of bread, honking a horn.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Goan breakfast and bar snack, and a sign of the Portuguese baker tradition.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sausages on a string, bread on a bicycle.

spotlights.name: Bebinca
spotlights.spot_it: A dense, dark brown pudding cut into slices that show many thin layers, like the rings of a tree.
spotlights.story_md: Bebinca is made of coconut milk, egg yolks, sugar and flour, baked one thin layer at a time, each layer browned under heat before the next is poured on. Traditionally there are seven to sixteen layers, and a 16-layer bebinca can take most of a day. A popular story says a nun named Bebiana invented it for a priest with seven layers for the seven hills of Lisbon; there is no evidence for this, and food historians treat it as legend. It is the centrepiece of the Christmas kuswar, the tray of sweets exchanged with neighbours.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The queen of Goan sweets.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sixteen layers, one at a time, one long day.

spotlights.name: Feni
spotlights.spot_it: A clear spirit with a strong fruity, slightly funky smell; the cashew version smells unmistakably of ripe cashew apples.
spotlights.story_md: The Portuguese brought cashew trees from Brazil to stop soil erosion. Goans found the fruit, the fleshy cashew apple, could be fermented and distilled. In March and April, fallen apples are crushed (traditionally by foot), the juice ferments for days, then is distilled in a clay or copper pot. The first distillate, urrak, is about 15 percent alcohol and sold fresh in summer. A second distillation gives feni, around 42 to 45 percent. Cashew feni got a Geographical Indication in 2009, and Goa named it a heritage spirit in 2016. Coconut feni, from palm toddy, is older.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's first liquor with a GI tag.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fruit that came from Brazil, a spirit that belongs to Goa.

sections.title: Festivals
sections.intro_md:
Goa's calendar has two kinds of crowd: villagers celebrating, and visitors watching them do it. Most festivals belong to one community but draw everyone.

The Catholic year runs from the Christmas kuswar to Carnival before Lent, then the monsoon feast of Sao Joao in June, when young men jump into flooded wells. The Hindu year has Ganesh Chaturthi, called Chovoth, the biggest family festival, when emigrants fly home; Shigmo, the spring festival, with drums and floats; and Diwali, which in Goa begins before dawn with burning a giant demon.

The state now runs the big ones as tourism events, with official float parades. Smaller village feasts are where the real thing is.

spotlights.name: Carnival
spotlights.spot_it: Float parades with masks, brass bands and dancers, led by a costumed 'King Momo' who decrees four days of fun.
spotlights.story_md: The Portuguese brought Carnival, the feast before the 40 days of Lent. In Goa it lasts four days, starting with the arrival of King Momo, a figure chosen each year, who orders people to eat, drink and be merry. Float parades roll through Panaji, Margao, Mapusa and Vasco, mixing satire, Konkani folk dances and advertising. Since the 1960s it has become a tourist event, and critics say much of the Catholic meaning is gone. The 2026 Panaji parade was on 14 February.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's best-known festival to the outside world.
spotlights.memory_hook: A king who orders you to party for four days.

spotlights.name: Shigmo

where.label: Panaji, Ponda, Mapusa, Vasco and villages

spotlights.spot_it: Troupes of men with huge drums (dhol and tasha), flags and tall decorated poles, followed by floats of gods and demons.
spotlights.story_md: Shigmo is the spring festival of Hindu Goa, linked to Holi but much older and longer. In villages, men's troupes go house to house with drums, songs and dances such as ghode modni, where dancers wear a wooden horse frame at the waist. The state organises float parades in towns, with giant figures from the epics. The festival also marks the return of warriors home after the winter campaigns. In 2026 the parades ran from 5 to 18 March at 19 centres.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Hindu counterpart to Carnival, louder and older.
spotlights.memory_hook: Drums, dummy horses and two weeks of spring.

spotlights.name: Sao Joao
spotlights.spot_it: Young men wearing crowns of leaves and fruit jump into overflowing wells and ponds, shouting 'Viva Sao Joao'.
spotlights.story_md: On the feast of St John the Baptist, 24 June, the monsoon is at its height and wells are full. The story is that John leapt for joy in his mother's womb when Mary visited, so Goans leap into wells. They wear kopels, crowns made of leaves, flowers and fruit. Newly married sons-in-law are expected to visit their in-laws. In Siolim, decorated boats and rafts sail on the river in a competition. Feni flows, which explains some of the jumping.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A monsoon festival found almost nowhere else in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A saint who leapt for joy, and a village that jumps in the well.

spotlights.name: Narkasur
spotlights.spot_it: Giant paper and straw demon effigies with fangs and horns, standing at street corners, burned before dawn.
spotlights.story_md: In Goa Diwali celebrates Krishna's killing of the demon Narakasura. For weeks, young men in each neighbourhood build Narkasur effigies, some more than 10 metres tall, from bamboo, straw, paper and paint, with fireworks inside. On the eve of Diwali they parade them through the streets, and around 4 am the effigies are burned. Families then take an early bath and eat bitter karit fruit to mark the victory. Competitions for the best Narkasur have grown into big events, with prizes and noise complaints.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's own version of Diwali, centred on a demon not on lamps.
spotlights.memory_hook: Build a demon for a month, burn it before dawn.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
Goa ranks at or near the top of Indian states on most quality-of-life measures: high income, long life expectancy, high literacy, and the highest Human Development Index rank in India. It has more registered vehicles per person than almost anywhere in India, and very few people without a home.

Goa also has unusual laws. It kept the Portuguese Civil Code of 1867 after 1961, so marriage, inheritance and property follow one law for all religions. A married couple shares property equally, and children inherit equally, sons and daughters. Goa was long the only Indian state with a common civil code; Uttarakhand adopted its own in January 2025.

Then there is susegad, the word outsiders use for the relaxed Goan pace, from the Portuguese sossegado, 'quiet'. Treat it carefully. Goa's literacy, income and emigration record do not describe a lazy people, and many Goans find the stereotype insulting. What it describes is the long lunch, the siesta and the shop shut from 1 to 4.

spotlights.name: The Goa civil code
spotlights.spot_it: No image: you see it in documents, in the requirement that couples register their marriage and agree on property.
spotlights.story_md: The Portuguese Civil Code of 1867 still governs family law in Goa, amended over time. Every marriage must be registered with the civil registrar, whatever the religion. Unless the couple agree otherwise before marrying, everything they own becomes joint property, split equally on divorce or death. Children inherit equally. Critics point out quirks: Hindu men in Goa could, in law, take a second wife if the first had no son by 25, a provision rarely used and widely mocked. It is often held up in national debates on a uniform civil code.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A working example of one family law for all religions.
spotlights.memory_hook: Married in Goa: half of everything is hers.

spotlights.name: Communidades
spotlights.spot_it: No image: the communidade is an office, a register and an annual meeting, not a building.
spotlights.story_md: Before Portugal, each Goan village was run by its gaunkars, descendants of the founding families, who held village land in common, leased it out, and shared income after paying for the temple, the school and the bunds. The Portuguese wrote down these customs in the Foral de Usos e Costumes of 1526 and renamed them communidades. There are about 220 of them still. They own large tracts of land, and fights over selling it for housing, golf courses and IT parks are among the hottest issues in Goan politics.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's ancient form of village self-rule, now at the centre of land fights.
spotlights.memory_hook: Village land that belongs to the village, on paper since 1526.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
For a state of 1.5 million, Goa has produced a long list of people India knows: singers, painters, cartoonists, scientists, an architect, a hypnotist and a defence minister. Many did their work outside Goa, in Bombay, London or Paris, which is also very Goan.

There are reasons. Catholic parishes taught music and Latin from the 1600s, and the Portuguese opened a medical school in Goa in 1842, one of the oldest in Asia. Hindu Goa had hereditary families of temple musicians and dancers, the Kalavant community, who produced several of the great classical singers of the 20th century. And Goa's ports pushed people out: to Bombay's offices and bands, to East Africa's civil services, to Lisbon's universities. The scientist Raghunath Mashelkar, the singer Hema Sardesai and the novelist Damodar Mauzo, who won the Jnanpith in 2022 for Konkani, belong on the list too. Below are seven to start with.

spotlights.name: Mario Miranda
spotlights.spot_it: Crowded black-ink cartoons of Bombay and Goa: fat bosses, glamorous secretaries, village priests, dogs, all lovingly mocked.
spotlights.story_md: Mario de Miranda drew for The Times of India group for decades, creating characters like Miss Fonseca and Godbole. He filled whole walls of Bombay cafes, most famously Cafe Mondegar in Colaba, with crowded scenes of city life. His Goa is affectionate: feasts, bands, buses, fat landlords. He was born in Daman and grew up in his ancestral house in Loutolim. He received the Padma Shri, Padma Bhushan and, after his death, the Padma Vibhushan in 2012.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He drew what Goa and Bombay look like to those who love them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every wall at Mondegar is a crowd he drew.

spotlights.name: Abbe Faria
spotlights.spot_it: In Panaji, a bronze statue of a priest leaning over a woman, his hands raised as if casting a spell.
spotlights.story_md: José Custódio de Faria was born in Candolim in 1756, became a priest, and in Paris became one of the first scientists of hypnosis. Against the fashionable idea of Mesmer's 'animal magnetism', he argued that the subject's own mind does the work: suggestion, not a mysterious fluid. Alexandre Dumas used his name for the old prisoner who teaches Edmond Dantès in The Count of Monte Cristo, though the fictional abbé has little to do with the real one. His statue stands beside the Adil Shah palace in Panaji.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Goan priest who helped invent the science of suggestion.
spotlights.memory_hook: The hypnotist from Candolim who ended up in Monte Cristo.

spotlights.name: F. N. Souza
spotlights.spot_it: Paintings of distorted faces and bodies drawn with thick black lines, angry saints, and nudes.
spotlights.story_md: Francis Newton Souza was born in Saligao and expelled from Bombay's St Xavier's College in 1939 for graffiti. In 1947 he founded the Progressive Artists' Group with S. H. Raza and M. F. Husain, the group that launched modern Indian art. He moved to London and then New York. His 1955 painting Birth sold in 2008 for 2.5 million dollars, then a record for an Indian painting, and again in 2015 for about 4 million. His Catholic upbringing is everywhere in his work, usually turned inside out.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The founder of the movement that made modern Indian art.
spotlights.memory_hook: Expelled for graffiti, founded a movement, sold for millions.

spotlights.name: Lata Mangeshkar's Goan roots
spotlights.spot_it: The voice of Hindi film for seven decades; her surname is a Goan place name.
spotlights.story_md: Lata Mangeshkar was born in Indore, but her father, the singer and actor Dinanath Mangeshkar, came from a family in Mangeshi in Goa, linked to the Mangueshi temple. He took the village's name as his surname. Lata, Asha Bhosle and their siblings all carry it. Through Dinanath and the Gomantak Maratha Samaj, the family belongs to Goa's long tradition of hereditary performing artists, the same tradition that produced Kesarbai Kerkar and Mogubai Kurdikar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's most famous voice carries the name of a Goan temple village.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mangeshkar means 'from Mangeshi'.

spotlights.name: Kishori Amonkar
spotlights.spot_it: A Hindustani classical singer known for intense, slow, emotional alap and a famously demanding stage manner.
spotlights.story_md: Kishori Amonkar was the daughter of Mogubai Kurdikar, the great singer of the Jaipur-Atrauli gharana, who was born in Curdi, the village now under the Salaulim reservoir. Kishori trained with her mother and then broke gharana rules, mixing styles in search of emotional truth. She was one of the most admired voices of 20th-century Indian classical music, received the Padma Vibhushan in 2002, and was known for stopping concerts if the audience did not listen properly.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A link between Goa's drowned village and India's concert halls.
spotlights.memory_hook: Her mother's village is under water; her voice is not.

spotlights.name: Manohar Parrikar
spotlights.spot_it: A Chief Minister in a half-sleeve shirt and sandals, often riding a scooter.
spotlights.story_md: Parrikar, a metallurgical engineer from IIT Bombay, was the first IIT graduate to become a Chief Minister. He led Goa four times between 2000 and 2019 and served as India's Defence Minister from 2014 to 2017, when the 2016 cross-border strikes were carried out. Known for a plain lifestyle, he rode a scooter and queued at airports. He died in office of pancreatic cancer on 17 March 2019. Goa's new airport at Mopa, opened in 2023, is named after him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's most influential politician since statehood.
spotlights.memory_hook: From IIT to Defence Minister, on a scooter.

spotlights.name: Charles Correa
spotlights.spot_it: Low, open buildings with courtyards and pergolas, designed for heat and rain; in Panaji, the Kala Academy on the river.
spotlights.story_md: Charles Correa, of a Goan family, became one of India's greatest architects, known for the Gandhi Smarak Sangrahalaya at Sabarmati, Jawahar Kala Kendra in Jaipur and the planning of Navi Mumbai. In Goa he designed the Kala Academy (1983), the state's arts centre on the Mandovi, and the Cidade de Goa hotel. His idea was 'open to sky' space, rooms and courtyards that let the climate in. He won the Royal Institute of British Architects gold medal in 1984.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The architect who designed for Indian weather, not against it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Open to sky, open to the river.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Most visitors never leave the strip of beach from Candolim to Anjuna. The rest of Goa is a short drive away: forts on headlands, quiet southern bays, Ponda's temples, Old Goa's churches, and the hills.

The north is busy and built-up: Calangute, Baga, Anjuna, Vagator and Morjim, with clubs and markets. The south is quieter: Colva and Benaulim in Salcete, then Agonda, Palolem and Galgibaga in Canacona, where olive ridley turtles nest. Go between November and March for beaches, between June and September for green hills and waterfalls.

spotlights.name: Chapora fort
spotlights.spot_it: Low, broken red laterite walls on a bare hill above the Chapora river mouth and Vagator beach.
spotlights.story_md: The fort was built by Adil Shah and rebuilt by the Portuguese in 1717 to guard the northern frontier. It changed hands with the Marathas more than once. Today there is almost nothing inside the walls, but the view over the river, the fishing harbour and Vagator beach is the best in North Goa. Its fame is recent: the 2001 Hindi film Dil Chahta Hai filmed a scene of its three friends sitting on the wall here, and many visitors now come to recreate it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A ruined fort made famous by a film.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three friends on a wall, and a whole generation came to copy them.

spotlights.name: Anjuna and the flea market
spotlights.when: Hippies from the 1960s; market weekly in season
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of stalls under trees selling clothes, jewellery, spices and Tibetan, Kashmiri and Lamani crafts, every Wednesday in season.
spotlights.story_md: In the 1960s Anjuna and Calangute were stops on the hippie trail from Europe to Kathmandu. Travellers who ran out of money sold their belongings at a weekly market, which grew into the Anjuna flea market, now run on Wednesdays from November to April. The full-moon parties of the 1970s and 1980s gave rise to Goa trance, a fast psychedelic electronic music that went global in the 1990s. Today noise rules after 10 pm have shifted most of the night scene indoors and to Vagator.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Where Goa's international reputation as a hippie haven began.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hippies sold their jeans here; now everyone sells everything.

spotlights.name: Cabo de Rama
spotlights.spot_it: A gate in a long laterite wall on a high cliff, a small white church inside, and the open sea beyond.
spotlights.story_md: Legend says Rama stayed here with Sita during his exile, which gives the cape its name. The fort belonged to Hindu rulers, then Muslim, then the Portuguese took it in 1763 during the New Conquests. Inside the walls there is a small church still used for Mass, and a few rusty cannons. The cliffs fall straight into the Arabian Sea. It is one of the emptiest and most dramatic places on the Goan coast.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A fort at the end of the road, with the best sea views in the south.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rama's cape, Portugal's fort, nobody's crowd.

sections.title: How Goa earns
sections.intro_md:
Goa's economy rests on three legs. Tourism: 10.8 million arrivals in 2025, of whom about 518,000 were foreign, plus hotels, shacks, taxis and casinos. Mining: iron ore from the hills, exported mostly to China and Japan through Mormugao port. Manufacturing: pharmaceuticals, especially around Verna and Kundaim, which make Goa one of the biggest drug-producing states per head.

Mining was the money of the 1990s and 2000s, and the scandal. In 2012 the Justice M. B. Shah Commission estimated illegal mining losses at around 35,000 crore rupees. The Supreme Court stopped all mining in October 2012, allowed a capped restart in 2014, then quashed 88 leases in February 2018. Mining stopped again. Since 2023 the state has auctioned blocks, and by July 2025 three of 12 auctioned mines were operating.

The per capita income was about 7.38 lakh rupees in 2024-25 by the state's quick estimate, second only to Sikkim on the latest national comparison.

spotlights.name: Iron ore and Mormugao
spotlights.spot_it: Long trains and barges of red-brown ore, red dust on roadside trees in Bicholim and Sanguem.
spotlights.story_md: Goa's iron ore is low grade but cheap to dig and close to the sea, so it was exported almost entirely, by river barge to Mormugao and onto ships. At its peak around 2010 Goa exported over 40 million tonnes a year. Mining towns grew rich and dusty; hills were cut away and rivers silted. The 2012 Shah Commission report on illegal mining led to the Supreme Court ban. Mining families, truck owners and barge workers have campaigned for a restart ever since, and environmentalists against.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's second economy, and its biggest environmental scar.
spotlights.memory_hook: Red hills, red trucks, red trees, and a ban.

spotlights.name: Manohar International Airport, Mopa
spotlights.spot_it: A new airport terminal in the far north of Goa, about 35 kilometres from Panaji, with long roofs of local laterite colour.
spotlights.story_md: For decades Goa's only airport was Dabolim, which is also an Indian Navy airbase, INS Hansa, so civilian flights were limited. A second airport at Mopa in Pernem, built by GMR and named after Manohar Parrikar, opened in January 2023. It handled about 5.4 million passengers in April 2025 to March 2026, up nearly 16 percent. Taxi unions, Dabolim's South Goa users and North Goa landowners have all fought over which airport gets which flights. In October 2026 Goa cut its VAT on jet fuel to 7 percent to attract airlines.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Goa's new front door, and a fight between north and south.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two airports, one of them a Navy base.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
Goa's news in 2025 and 2026 has been about crowds, safety, land and the next election.

On 3 May 2025 a crush at the Lairai jatra in Shirgao killed six people. On 6 December 2025 a fire at the nightclub Birch by Romeo Lane in Arpora, North Goa, killed 25 people, most of them kitchen staff. The club had violated fire rules, and a demolition order had been withdrawn; the state ordered a magisterial inquiry and audits of other clubs.

On 31 December 2025 the state notified Kushavati as its third district, made of Quepem, Sanguem, Dharbandora and Canacona, with headquarters at Quepem. By March 2026 it still lacked full offices.

Tourist arrivals hit a record 10.8 million in 2025. On 6 August 2026 a central law came into force to reserve Assembly seats for Scheduled Tribes, likely four of 40, before the Assembly election expected in February 2027. In October 2026 Goa cut VAT on aviation fuel to 7 percent.

spotlights.name: The Arpora nightclub fire
spotlights.spot_it: No image used: a two-storey club with palm-leaf decorations near the Baga river.
spotlights.story_md: Shortly before midnight on 6 December 2025 a fire broke out at Birch by Romeo Lane, a club in Arpora. Twenty-five people died and about 50 were injured; 20 of the dead were staff. Reports pointed to indoor fireworks or a gas cylinder, with dry palm-leaf decor helping the fire spread. The narrow lane kept fire engines at a distance. The Chief Minister said the club had broken fire safety rules, and it emerged that a demolition notice for building without a permit had been withdrawn. It became the deadliest fire in Goa's recent history.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It forced a reckoning on how Goa's party economy is regulated.
spotlights.memory_hook: Palm leaves, fireworks, one narrow lane.

spotlights.name: Kushavati district
spotlights.spot_it: A new name on Goa's map: the hilly south-east, named after the river that runs past the Usgalimal carvings.
spotlights.story_md: Kushavati is Goa's third district, carved out of South Goa. It covers Quepem, Sanguem, Dharbandora and Canacona, the mostly rural, forested and tribal south-east, where many people felt Margao's offices were too far away and too focused on the coast. The ruling BJP called it decentralisation; critics questioned the cost and whether a state of 1.5 million needed three districts. Two months after it was notified, residents were still going to Margao for many services.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first change to Goa's map since statehood.
spotlights.memory_hook: A river that once hid rock art now names a district.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
Goa attracts more stories than almost any Indian state. Some are true, many are not.

**Myth: Goa is a Christian state.** Fact: two-thirds of Goans are Hindu (66.1 percent in 2011). Christians are a quarter.

**Myth: Goa was part of British India.** Fact: it was Portuguese, and stayed so 14 years after 1947.

**Myth: Goans are lazy (susegad).** Fact: Goa has among the highest literacy, incomes and emigration rates in India. Susegad describes a pace of life, not a work ethic.

**Myth: vindaloo has potatoes.** Fact: the name comes from vinho and alhos, wine and garlic.

**Myth: Goans all speak Portuguese.** Fact: very few do today. The language of daily life is Konkani, then English, Hindi and Marathi.

**Myth: Bebinca was invented by a nun called Bebiana.** Fact: a nice story with no evidence.

**Myth: Goa has always been the party capital.** Fact: the party scene is a product of the 1960s hippie trail. Most Goans have never been to a beach party.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
**Where:** India's smallest state, 3,702 km², on the west coast between Maharashtra and Karnataka. 1.46 million people in 2011. Capital Panaji. Three districts since December 2025.

**When:** Kadambas from about 960. Portugal from 1510 to 1961, 451 years. Operation Vijay, 18 to 19 December 1961. Opinion Poll, 16 January 1967: Goa stays separate. Statehood 30 May 1987.

**What to recognise:** red laterite Bom Jesus with Xavier's silver casket; the one-towered Se; temple lamp towers (deepastambha) in Ponda; painted houses with a balcao in Fontainhas; oyster-shell windows; the clay ghumot drum.

**What to eat:** fish curry rice; vindaloo (wine and garlic, no potato); xacuti; sorpotel with sannas; green cafreal; chourico in pao; bebinca; cashew feni (GI 2009).

**Festivals:** Carnival, Shigmo, Sao Joao (jump in the well), Narkasur before Diwali, Chovoth.

**People:** Mario Miranda, Abbe Faria, F. N. Souza, Kishori Amonkar, the Mangeshkars, Charles Correa, Manohar Parrikar.

**Now:** record 10.8 million tourists in 2025, the Arpora fire, Kushavati district, mining's slow restart, an election due in early 2027.

best_facts.fact: A Goan village, Curdi, drowned by the Salaulim dam, rises out of the reservoir every summer and its former residents return to hold a temple festival on the dry bed.
best_facts.why_surprising: A village with a seasonal existence.

best_facts.fact: India's first printing press arrived in Goa in 1556 by accident: it was on its way to Ethiopia.
best_facts.why_surprising: A detour that started printing in India.

best_facts.fact: Garcia de Orta's book on Indian drugs was printed in Goa in 1563; in 1580 the Inquisition dug up his bones and burned them because he was of Jewish descent.
best_facts.why_surprising: Celebrated and posthumously burned by the same colony.

best_facts.fact: Goa is the only Indian territory whose future was decided by a direct popular vote: on 16 January 1967 Goans rejected merger with Maharashtra, 172,191 to 138,170.
best_facts.why_surprising: India rarely asks people to vote on borders.

best_facts.fact: Portugal ruled Goa for 451 years; India took it in about 36 hours in December 1961, and the Portuguese governor surrendered against Salazar's direct orders.
best_facts.why_surprising: Centuries ended in a day and a half.

best_facts.fact: Vindaloo is from the Portuguese carne de vinha d'alhos, meat in wine and garlic. The 'aloo' is not potato.
best_facts.why_surprising: A British curry-house staple has a Portuguese name.

best_facts.fact: St Francis Xavier died in 1552, yet about 8 million people came to see his body in Old Goa in 2024 and 2025.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 16th-century saint still draws Goa's biggest crowd.

best_facts.fact: Old Goa's houses and churches used polished windowpane-oyster shells instead of glass.
Lata Mangeshkar's surname comes from Mangeshi, a Goan temple village her father's family came from.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's most famous voice has a Goan address in her name.

best_facts.fact: The trains on the Londa to Vasco line cross the face of Dudhsagar Falls on a bridge, inside the spray.
Chillies, cashews, potatoes, tomatoes, papayas and pineapples all reached India through the Portuguese, mostly via Goa.
Abbe Faria, a priest from Candolim, was a pioneer of hypnosis and gave his name to a character in The Count of Monte Cristo.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Goan in a French classic.

best_facts.fact: Two-thirds of Goans are Hindu; Christians were 25.1 percent in 2011.
Goan temples in Ponda borrowed from churches: domes, chandeliers and a lamp tower in place of a bell tower.
best_facts.why_surprising: Temples designed in conversation with the Baroque.

best_facts.fact: Cashew feni was the first Indian liquor to get a Geographical Indication, in 2009.
best_facts.why_surprising: A spirit, protected like Darjeeling tea.

best_facts.fact: Goa's family law is still based on the Portuguese Civil Code of 1867: one law for all religions, with spouses sharing property equally.
best_facts.why_surprising: A uniform civil code has existed in India since 1961.

best_facts.fact: The first printed book in Konkani, in 1622, was written by an English Jesuit, Thomas Stephens.
best_facts.why_surprising: An Englishman, decades before the East India Company arrived in force.

best_facts.fact: On Sao Joao, 24 June, young Goan men jump into flooded wells to honour John the Baptist, who 'leapt' in his mother's womb.
best_facts.why_surprising: A literal reading of scripture as a festival.

verification.claim: Age of the Usgalimal rock engravings
verification.note: Estimates range from about 4,000 to 6,000 years (Wikipedia, Neolithic) to 20,000 to 30,000 years (travel sources). No published direct dating found.

verification.claim: Number of trials and executions by the Goa Inquisition
verification.note: About 16,000 trials is a commonly cited figure; executions run to the hundreds. Most records were destroyed after 1812.

verification.claim: When Curdi was fully submerged
verification.note: Sources give the 1970s (resettlement from 1971, dam work to about 1975) and 1986 (first full submergence).

verification.claim: Abbe Faria's date of death
verification.note: Wikipedia gives both 20 September and 30 September 1819.

verification.claim: Goa's coastline length
verification.note: Figures of about 105 km and 160 km both circulate, depending on whether estuaries are counted. Not stated in the text.

verification.claim: Goa's per capita income rank
verification.note: Second after Sikkim on 2023-24 MoSPI data. Goa's 2024-25 quick estimate (7.38 lakh rupees) has no full national comparison yet.

verification.claim: Mopa airport passengers April 2025 to March 2026
verification.note: 5.38 million taken from the Wikipedia infobox citing AAI; not checked on the AAI site.

verification.claim: Cause of the Arpora nightclub fire
verification.note: Police first cited a gas cylinder blast; later reports pointed to indoor fireworks igniting palm-leaf decor. Inquiry outcome not checked.

verification.claim: Injuries at the Shirgao stampede, 3 May 2025
verification.note: Reports range from 30 to about 80 injured; one outlet gave seven deaths, most say six.

verification.claim: Painting law for Goan houses under Portugal
verification.note: Widely repeated that owners had to repaint after each monsoon or pay a fine; no primary source found.

verification.claim: Number of beach shack licences per season
verification.note: 350 to 400 is an approximate range from tourism policy reporting; varies by year.

side_dish.title: Abbe Faria and the power of suggestion
side_dish.body_md:
In 1814 Paris was full of magnetisers. Followers of Franz Mesmer claimed an invisible fluid, 'animal magnetism', flowed from their hands into patients, sending them into trances and curing them. A priest from Candolim, José Custódio de Faria, opened his own lecture-demonstrations and said something radical: there is no fluid.

Faria seated his subjects in a chair, asked them to close their eyes and relax, then said firmly, 'Sleep.' Many did, in a state he called **lucid sleep**. His conclusion: the cause lies in the subject, not the magnetiser. Some people are more ready than others to accept an idea and act on it. He called the key ingredient **concentration** and the subject's readiness. Today we call it **suggestibility**.

That shift, from a force in the healer to a process in the patient's mind, is the root of modern hypnosis and of research on the placebo effect. A sugar pill works partly because you expect it to. An anxious patient told 'this will sting a little' feels more pain than one told 'you may feel pressure'.

Faria was mocked in his lifetime, and an actor staged a fake trance to embarrass him. He died poor in 1819. His book, On the Cause of Lucid Sleep, was rediscovered decades later by the Nancy school of hypnosis.

Try it: the next time a doctor, teacher or ad tells you how something will feel, notice the suggestion inside the sentence.

offline_task.title: Cook a Goan fish curry tonight
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 3. About 40 minutes.**

**You need**
- 500 g firm fish (kingfish, mackerel, pomfret) or prawns, cut and rubbed with salt and turmeric
- 1 cup grated coconut (fresh or frozen)
- 6 to 8 dried Kashmiri red chillies (for colour), 2 hot ones if you like heat
- 1 teaspoon coriander seeds, half a teaspoon cumin, 4 peppercorns, 3 cloves garlic, a thumb of ginger, half a teaspoon turmeric
- 4 to 5 kokum petals, or a small ball of tamarind soaked in water
- 1 small onion, sliced; 1 green chilli, slit; salt; 2 tablespoons coconut oil

**Steps**
1. Grind the coconut, red chillies, coriander, cumin, peppercorns, garlic, ginger and turmeric with about 1 cup of water to a smooth, bright orange paste.
2. Heat the oil, fry the onion until soft and golden.
3. Add the paste and 1 more cup of water. Simmer for 8 to 10 minutes until the raw smell goes and oil shows at the edges.
4. Add the kokum (or tamarind water), green chilli and salt. Simmer 2 minutes.
5. Slide in the fish. Cook gently for 5 to 7 minutes without stirring hard. Turn off the heat when the fish is just opaque.
6. Rest 10 minutes. Eat with rice, ideally red parboiled rice, and a fried piece of fish on the side.

**Notice**: the curry should be thin, sour and orange, not thick and brown. That sourness, from kokum or tamarind, is the Goan signature.
